transcript.text: Long-Run Macroeconomic Self-Adjustment
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-36
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace wage and input-price adjustment that returns output toward potential.
Difficulty: Advanced
THE CORE IDEA

A recessionary gap has short-run output below potential; an inflationary gap has output above potential. With no new demand shock or discretionary policy, labor-market and input-price adjustment changes short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) over time. Weak demand for labor in a recessionary gap reduces wage-cost pressure and shifts SRAS right; an inflationary gap raises wage-cost pressure and shifts SRAS left. Output returns toward potential, marked by long-run aggregate supply (LRAS).
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare short-run equilibrium output with the LRAS position to classify the gap.
Below potential: wages and input costs adjust downward, shifting SRAS right.
Above potential: wages and input costs adjust upward, shifting SRAS left.
Self-adjustment changes SRAS; discretionary stabilization deliberately shifts AD.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume aggregate demand must reverse itself. In the textbook self-correction mechanism, wage and input-price adjustment shifts SRAS along the existing AD curve.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CLOSING A RECESSIONARY GAP

Horizontal axis: real output Y; vertical axis: price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. Downward-sloping AD1 is left of AD2. Upward-sloping AS1 is above and left of AS2. AS1 meets AD2 on LRAS at Y1 and P3; AS1 meets AD1 at Y3 and P2, left of LRAS. AS2 meets AD1 on LRAS at Y1 and P1, and meets AD2 at Y2 and P2, right of LRAS. The displayed ordering is Y3, Y1, Y2 from left to right, and P1, P2, P3 from bottom to top. Dashed guides mark these levels.

After AD falls to AD1, the short-run equilibrium is Y3, left of LRAS at Y1. Elevated unemployment reduces wage and input-cost pressure, shifting SRAS from AS1 to AS2. The economy moves along AD1 to Y1 at the lower price level P1 without discretionary policy.
CHECK YOURSELF
Output is above potential and AD is unchanged. Which direction must SRAS move during self-adjustment?

Disinflation and Policy
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-40
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace monetary disinflation, unemployment costs, and expectations adjustment.
Difficulty: Advanced
THE CORE IDEA

Disinflation lowers the inflation rate but usually creates temporary output and employment costs while expectations adjust. Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment. Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Disinflation means the inflation rate is falling, not that the price level is falling.
Contractionary policy initially moves the economy along the existing short-run Phillips curve toward higher unemployment.
As expected inflation falls, the short-run Phillips curve shifts downward.
Credible policy and flexible expectations can reduce the output and employment cost of lowering inflation.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse a lower positive inflation rate with a falling price level. Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.
WORKED EXAMPLE: LOWERING INFLATION

Horizontal axis: unemployment rate; vertical axis: inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower, leftward downward-sloping curve; SRPC2 is the higher, rightward downward-sloping curve. Point a on SRPC1 is at unemployment U1 and inflation I2. Point b, where SRPC2 meets LRPC, is at U2 and I2. Point c, where SRPC1 meets LRPC, is at U2 and I1. Point d on SRPC2 is at U3 and I1. From left to right the unemployment labels are U1, U2, U3; I2 is above I1. Dashed guides identify all four points. No numerical rates are printed.

Contractionary policy first moves the economy along SRPC2 from b to d, lowering inflation from I2 to I1 while unemployment rises from U2 to U3. As expected inflation adjusts downward, SRPC shifts to SRPC1 and unemployment returns to U2 at point c. Disinflation creates a temporary employment cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
Inflation falls from 5% to 2% but remains positive. Did the price level fall?
